uses: Burdock root is an old alterative, the herbalists' word for a plant believed to slowly set the body to rights, and Grieve ranked it high for long-lasting skin troubles such as eczema and boils. In folk practice the root and seed were boiled into drinks taken to increase urine. The EMA recognizes traditional use of the root to flush the urinary tract, to help a passing loss of appetite, and for oily, flaky skin. Culpeper laid the bruised leaves on burns and old sores. The long root is still eaten as a vegetable in Japan and Korea, and peeled young stalks were once boiled like asparagus.
taste: Root sweetish and slippery; leaves somewhat bitter
energetics: Culpeper called the leaves cooling and moderately drying
caution_pregnancy: The EMA does not recommend burdock during pregnancy or breastfeeding because there isn't enough data. MSK warns that it may stimulate the uterus and should be avoided in pregnancy; that warning comes from animal experiments, and the EMA found no human reports confirming it. Not enough is known; avoid.
caution_medications: The EMA advises against taking burdock root alongside prescription diuretics (water pills). No interaction with diabetes medicines is documented, but burdock root lowered blood sugar in animal studies and one small human study, so as a precaution ask your prescriber first if you take them and watch for lows. The EMA reports no other interactions.
caution_conditions: Do not use it if you are allergic to daisy-family (Asteraceae) plants; people allergic to chrysanthemums may react to burdock. Anaphylaxis has been reported, once in a man an hour after eating boiled burdock. A woman had acute liver injury after drinking a detox tea that contained it. Use isn't established for anyone under 18. Drink plenty of fluids while using it, and see a doctor if urinary symptoms bring fever, pain, cramps or blood. Burdock tea has been contaminated with deadly nightshade (belladonna) root, causing atropine poisoning, and the root can be mixed up with comfrey or dock; buy from a careful supplier and never dig it unless you are sure of the plant.
caution_duration: If urinary or appetite complaints last more than 2 weeks, or skin complaints more than 4 weeks, or anything gets worse, see a doctor or qualified practitioner.
caution_topical: The hooked burs and their bristles can irritate the eyes, skin and airways, so wear gloves around seed heads. Allergic contact dermatitis from burdock has been reported.
garden_harvest_timing: Dig roots from first-year plants before they turn woody; cultivated roots are lifted by late autumn, and Grieve's growers dug them in July. Pick young leaves and flower stalks before the plant blooms.
garden_water: Moist, well-drained, rich soil; a light soil gives the best roots
notes: A biennial: a low rosette the first year, then a tall flowering stem in the second. It self-seeds aggressively and its deep taproot makes it hard to remove, so many gardeners treat it as an invasive weed. The burs travel on fur and clothing and have trapped and killed small birds and bats. Bees take its nectar. Lesser burdock (Arctium minus) is often confused with it. Grieve traces the name Arctium to the Greek for bear, after the rough burs. Culpeper places burdock under Venus.
